faqs.question: What has to fit on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: A concrete match and one join control for the side you need first. The label should say who is joining. The other side can have a text link or a menu item. If the visitor must scroll to learn what the market is, the desktop layout has been allowed to decide the phone page.

faqs.question: Which speed targets matter for that first screen?
faqs.answer: web.dev's good thresholds are a practical brief: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. The hero should not shove the button aside after load, and the join control should respond as a tap, not as a wait. Test on a mid-range phone.

faqs.question: Should the mobile site use different navigation labels?
faqs.answer: No. Use the same job labels as the rest of the site, including the same words for the join path. A shorter, vaguer mobile menu creates a second information architecture. Sign in and apply should stay visually distinct so a thumb does not hit the wrong one.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The two-sided marketplace mobile website is the visit that counts. The side you need first will judge the company on a phone, often between two other tasks, and the first screen still has to show a concrete match and a way to join. Do not let the desktop composition decide that screen.

Design the phone page as the page. The wide layout is an adaptation, not the original.

## The first screen on a phone

Open the phone and look at what fits before any scroll. You need the match, in words and in a picture that still contains the evidence after the crop, and the join control, with a label that says which side is joining. The company name can be small. The mission line can wait.

If the match is a picture that becomes a vague interior once it is cropped, rewrite the frame or move the facts into the first lines of type. "Eight seats. Tuesday. Host keeps the menu." can sit in three lines beside a tight crop. A desktop headline that wraps into six lines on a phone has already spent the screen.

Nielsen Norman Group's finding still applies in a thumb's reach. People often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and value has to be clear within about 10. On a phone those seconds include the time the page takes to become stable. A hero that jumps, a font that arrives late and reflows the button, or a banner that pushes the match down will spend the visit before the sentence lands.

Put the join control where a thumb can reach it without covering the match. A bar pinned to the bottom can work if it does not hide the fee or the constraint. A button stranded in a desktop hero, which on the phone sits below two logos and a paragraph, is a button for people who already decided.

## What desktop habits break

A two-column hero that puts the sentence on the left and the proof on the right will stack in an order you did not choose, unless you choose it. Decide the stack. Proof, then sentence, then button. Or sentence, then proof, then button. Do not let the framework decide because that was the DOM order from a desktop frame in Figma.

Equal buttons become a taller problem on a phone. Two stacked calls to action occupy the entire decision area and still refuse to say which side you need. Keep one primary control. Put the other side in a text link under it, or in the menu. The menu is allowed to contain both doors. The first screen is not.

Hover menus, tiny footnotes, and tooltips that explain the fee do not exist for this visitor. If the shape of the price matters, it has to be in the first or second screen as text. "Fee taken from the host payout after the dinner" can be one line. A dotted underline that reveals it on hover is a secret.

Carousels, background video, and entrance animation are the usual ways a desktop comp tries to feel finished. On a phone they delay the match and move the button. Ship the still. If a motion treatment remains, it should be short, and it should honor a reduced-motion setting rather than being the only way to understand the page.

## Speed is part of the first screen

web.dev defines the current good thresholds for the three Core Web Vitals: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. Those numbers are a useful brief for this visit, because the first screen is the largest thing on it, the join control is the interaction, and a layout that shifts will make someone tap the wrong side.

Treat the hero image as a budget. A photograph of the match should be sized for the phone, not delivered as a desktop original the browser scales down. The words of the match should be HTML, so they are visible before the image finishes, and so they remain if the image fails. Text baked into the picture is invisible to that rule and fragile when you change a fee.

A pinned banner for a conference, a cookie wall that covers the button, and a chat widget that arrives late are layout shift and attention shift together. If you need a consent notice, keep it short and out of the join path. If you need chat, do not let it be the first thing a new host taps.

Test on a mid-range phone over a ordinary connection, not only on the laptop you designed with. The page can feel instant in a local preview and still miss the opening on the network your carriers or hosts actually use. Fix the opening before you add a section.

## The second screen has a job

After the match and the join path, the next screen answers the first objection. For many scarce-side visitors that objection is "what do you take, and what do I still have to do?" One fee line and three steps. Then a second match, or the constraint from a proof page, with a repeated join control.

Do not use the second screen to restate the mission in larger type. They have already paid you the first screen. The second screen is for the boundary: cities, credentials, what you refuse, how fast you reply. A boundary they can read with one thumb is a reason to continue. A manifesto is a reason to switch apps.

Forms that start on the phone should ask for the smallest set that lets you respond. Name, the city or the lane, and a way to reach them are often enough for a first reply. A ten-field application on a glass keyboard is how you lose the careful applicant in a parking lot. Save the rest for a step they reach after they know you will answer.

The menu on this screen still uses the job labels from the site map. Do not invent a shorter, vaguer set for mobile. "Menu" can open "Fees," "A real night," and "Apply as a host." It should not open "Explore."

## Review it like a stranger

Hold the phone at arm's length and read only what is sharp without zooming. Then hand it to someone from the scarce side and ask three questions. What is the match. What would you tap. What do you think it costs. If any answer is missing, it is not in the first two screens, and the desktop page cannot bail you out. They will not go find the desktop page.

Watch for accidental taps. Controls too close together, especially Sign in and Apply, will be mis-hit. Give the primary control clear space. Make the secondary path a text link with enough padding, not a second button of almost the same color.

Check the page in bright outdoor light if that is where this side lives. Drivers, hosts leaving a market, techs between jobs. Low-contrast gray on a photograph will disappear. The match and the button need contrast that survives glare. This is also basic perceivability, not a polish pass.

Do a pass with the largest phone text size the system allows. If the join label truncates or the match wraps over the button, the layout is not finished. A layout that only works at the default size works for the team and not for the applicant who needs larger type.

## Build the phone page as the source

In the design file, start the frame at a phone width. Write the first screen there. Only then ask how the same blocks sit on a wide monitor. A wide screen can add a margin, a second column of proof, or a larger crop. It should not add a different argument.

When the site is built, the phone layout is the one you test in review. Hanabi builds these pages in the browser, in Next.js, because a static desktop comp cannot tell you whether the button jumps when the type loads. Review on a device. File the bugs against the first screen before you debate the footer.

Keep one join URL. Campaigns, the header, and the first screen should hit the same short path. A mobile-only form that asks different questions from the desktop form will fill your inbox with two kinds of leads and no shared definition of "ready."

Read the first screen once in a mobile browser, not only in a design tool. A frame can lie about font loading, image weight, and the browser chrome that steals the top of the page. The address bar and the bottom gesture area are part of the layout. If the join control sits under the gesture bar, move it.

Keep a short written checklist for release: match visible without scroll, one join label, fee shape on the next screen, no second button of equal weight, no layout jump when the picture arrives. Run it on the production URL. A preview link on the office wifi is a different product from the page a host opens in a stairwell.

The tap has to land somewhere that tells them what happens next. A first screen that keeps its promise and a contact path that opens into ten unexplained fields will still lose the person. That path is [a contact path for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-two-sided-marketplace).

For a sense of how a public site can stay clear when the screen gets narrow, look through [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
